title: Remembering Gary Hufbauer
gist: Steven R. Weisman's PIIE tribute to Gary Clyde Hufbauer (died at 87), the trade, sanctions and subsidies economist behind Economic Sanctions Reconsidered's 'nine commandments' and the controversial '$1 trillion' (later $2 trillion+) US trade-gains estimate. It is a memorial piece with limited forward-looking content; the substantive takeaways are on sanctions design, NAFTA politics, and the defense of rough policy quantification against macro purists.

insights.claim: Gary Hufbauer and Jeff Schott's PIIE book Economic Sanctions Reconsidered (early 1980s) set out 'nine commandments' for using economic sanctions, including working with allies and focusing on limited targets.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Multilateral coordination and narrow targeting remain the benchmark tests for judging whether a sanctions regime is likely to bite.

themes.theme: Quantifying trade gains and the macro-vs-micro debate

insights.claim: Hufbauer's PIIE 'big number' estimate put gains to the US economy from trade expansion at $1 trillion, later updated to more than $2 trillion in 2017.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: A widely cited headline figure used in US trade-policy advocacy; it was controversial among academic economists.
insights.locator: The best examples, cited by Fred

insights.claim: According to C. Fred Bergsten, critics of Hufbauer-Schott NAFTA job-loss/gain estimates who argued there could be no job losses at full employment were confusing macro and micro economics; sector-level job estimates are necessary to inform policy debates even at full employment.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Trade-policy debates turn on localized, sectoral dislocation, not just aggregate employment; aggregate-only analysis misses the political economy.
insights.quote: "But the critics were confusing macro and micro economics. Those estimates by Gary were vitally necessary to inform policy debates."
insights.locator: The best examples, cited by Fred

insights.claim: Bergsten credited Hufbauer with willingness to make estimates and projections that would not pass muster with some PhD economists, arguing such rough quantification serves policymakers better than silence.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Policy-relevant think-tank output often trades academic rigor for timely, decision-useful numbers.
insights.quote: He was willing to go out on a limb and make estimates and projections even when he knew they weren't going to pass muster for some PhD economists.

themes.theme: Political economy of NAFTA and US trade policy

insights.claim: Former USTR Carla Hills said making the case for NAFTA in the 1990s was politically tough because both labor unions and the agriculture community opposed it, and Hufbauer's essays were important in persuading people.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Organized labor and agriculture are recurring veto constituencies in US trade-agreement politics; credible quantitative advocacy helped overcome them.
insights.quote: "Labor unions were not in favor, the agriculture community was not in favor. Gary's essays were important in persuading people.

insights.claim: Hufbauer and Schott began as part of the US Treasury team negotiating GATT subsidies agreements in the 1970s; Hufbauer later served as deputy assistant secretary for trade and investment under C. Fred Bergsten in the Carter-era Treasury before joining the Institute Bergsten founded in the early 1980s.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Illustrates the revolving door between Treasury trade negotiators and PIIE that shaped the institute's policy influence.

insights.claim: Trade historian Douglas Irwin called Hufbauer, together with Jeff Schott, a critical component of PIIE's early success, noting he combined a sense for both the economics and politics of trade.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: PIIE's trade-policy reputation was built on pairing economics with political feasibility.
insights.quote: "I studied the history of US trade policy, but he lived much of it, and he had a great sense for both the economics and politics of trade."

themes.theme: Legacy, intellectual lineage and mentorship network

insights.claim: Hufbauer, who died in November 2026 at 87, was an expert on subsidies, sanctions, trade and tax policy and produced work at the Peterson Institute for more than 40 years; PIIE president Adam Posen called his work a pillar of the Institute's reputation.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Loss of a leading voice on sanctions and trade at a major Washington trade think tank.

insights.claim: Hufbauer's intellectual formation at Harvard blended free-market libertarian Gottfried Haberler and Keynesian Seymour Harris, leading to a senior thesis on balance-of-payments issues and later Treasury work on payment imbalances.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Explains his pragmatic, non-doctrinaire approach to trade and payments policy.

insights.claim: Hufbauer's mentees now hold influential posts, including Daniel Rosen (founder of Rhodium Group), Cathleen Cimino-Isaacs (Congressional Research Service) and Barbara Kotschwar (director of economic development at the OAS).
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: His analytical style propagates through China-economy consultancy, Congressional research and multilateral development institutions.

insights.claim: Bob Davis of the Wall Street Journal described Hufbauer as one of the most honest people in Washington, not afraid to make a call and not afraid to admit a mistake.
insights.speaker: Steven R. Weisman
insights.so_what: Willingness to make falsifiable calls and revise them is presented as the hallmark of credible policy analysis.
insights.quote: "I considered him…one of the most honest people in Washington—not afraid to make a call and not afraid to admit to a mistake."
